speaker: Doctor
text: Please tell me your name and your age, as this is a pediatric patient. Also, when did the itchy rash first appear after starting the antibiotic treatment?

speaker: Patient
text: 8-year-old girl. The patient was brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of low-grade fever, itchy rash, and generalized joint pain. The rash initially started in the antecubital and popliteal fossae before spreading to the trunk and distal extremities. One week ago, she was diagnosed with acute sinusitis and started on amoxicillin. She has no history of adverse drug reactions, and her immunizations are up to date.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. Given the rash pattern and timing after amoxicillin, I suspect this might be a specific hypersensitivity reaction. Did you notice any swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, or any difficulty breathing when the rash appeared? REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Diagnosed with acute sinusitis one week ago, no known history of adverse drug reactions, immunizations up to date. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Patient
text: No additional symptoms mentioned. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is very strange, as the rash you described spreading from the joints to the trunk is not typical for appendicitis, which usually presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever without a generalized itchy rash. Did the rash change color to purple or red spots that do not fade when you press on them, and has your child had any difficulty moving their joints? REQUEST IMAGES: Dermoscopy of rash.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Amoxicillin-induced Morbilliform Drug Eruption with arthralgia. The clinical picture of a pruritic rash appearing 1 week after initiating amoxicillin, spreading from flexural areas to the trunk, accompanied by low-grade fever and joint pain, is classic for a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. The previous diagnosis of appendicitis was incorrect given the absence of localized peritoneal signs.
